name: Boots Soltan / star rating
lead: The Boots star rating is a UK and Ireland label that tells shoppers how much UVA protection a sunscreen gives relative to its UVB protection. For anyone trying to keep skin looking young, even-toned and free of sun spots, the stars are a quick way to see whether a sunscreen covers the UVA rays associated with photoageing, alongside the SPF number that reflects UVB.[1][6]

Wikipedia describes the system as a proprietary in vitro method in which five stars is the highest UVA ratio and one star the lowest.[1] Brian Diffey at Newcastle University did the original work and Boots in Nottingham developed the method, which many UK manufacturers adopted.[1] Soltan is Boots' own sunscreen range, which carries the rating on its packaging.

People using sunscreen as a looks tool, to limit tanning, pigmentation and premature lines, often look for a high star count together with a high SPF. The NHS advises choosing a sunscreen with at least SPF 30 and at least four UVA stars.[6] Research has also shown how much real-world products can differ: sunscreens with the same label SPF have been found to behave differently under sunlight, and UVA performance of popular products has varied.[2][3]

angle.text: People who want to keep skin youthful and even-toned use the star rating to pick a sunscreen that covers UVA as well as UVB. It is a shopping aid for daily sun protection rather than a treatment.

infobox: Look for SPF 30 or higher and at least 4 stars [6]
EU UVA seal; PA+ to PA++++ in East Asia [4]

paras: The star rating is a proprietary in vitro method, based on original work by Brian Diffey at Newcastle University and developed by the Boots Company in Nottingham. Many companies selling sunscreen in the UK have adopted it, which is why stars appear on products from many brands, not just Boots' own Soltan range.[1][4]

Originally one star marked the lowest UVA-to-UVB ratio and five stars the highest. Under the current methodology the range runs from three to five stars, with three the lowest.[4] In August 2007 the US FDA proposed a version of the protocol to inform American consumers about UVA protection but did not adopt it, reportedly because it could be confusing.[4]

The method compares UVA to UVB protection in vitro, measured with a spectrophotometer. After revision following the Colipa UVA PF test and updated EU recommendations, samples are pre-irradiated to better reflect in-use UVA protection, and the lowest rating became three stars.[1][4]

Separately, EU rules require UVA protection of at least one-third of the labelled SPF to carry the UVA seal, a circled 'UVA' logo, following European Commission Recommendation 2006/647/EC.[1][6] To count as broad-spectrum in the EU a product needs a UVA/UVB ratio of at least one-third and a critical wavelength of at least 370 nm, and sunscreens are regulated as cosmetics rather than as over-the-counter drugs.[1] SPF itself was introduced in 1974 by Franz Greiter, and EU labels cap at 50+.[1]

The NHS describes SPF as a measure of UVB protection and the star rating as a measure of UVA protection, with up to five stars in the UK; it also notes that most people do not apply enough sunscreen, suggesting about six to eight teaspoons for the whole body of an adult, with reapplication about every two hours and after swimming or sweating.[6]

In the Sun protection factor article, Wikipedia describes the revision as adding pre-irradiation of samples, which it says better indicates UVA protection and photostability during use. SPF itself was introduced in 1974 by Franz Greiter, adapting earlier calculations by Friedrich Ellinger and Rudolf Schulze; an SPF figure assumes application at 2 mg per square centimetre and says little about UVA.[4]

UVA penetrates deeper than UVB and contributes to invisible skin damage, which is why UVA labelling matters to people concerned about lines, sagging and dark spots.[1] Wikipedia's sunscreen article reports a 2013 Australian trial of about 900 people in which daily broad-spectrum sunscreen over four and a half years was linked to smoother, more resilient skin than in controls, and a study of 32 volunteers in which daily SPF 30 use was associated with reversal of photoageing signs over 12 weeks.[1]
Because people typically apply only a quarter to half of the amount used in SPF testing, the effective protection is lower than the label figure, according to the same article.[1]

The NHS gives SPF a scale of 2 to 50+ for UVB and says UK sunscreens show up to five stars for UVA, with more stars better. It recommends at least SPF 30, applying sunscreen about 30 minutes before going out and again just before, and reapplying every two hours and after swimming, towel drying or sweating, even with water-resistant products.[6] Together, a high SPF and a high star count describe protection against both burning and the deeper-penetrating UVA associated with photoageing.[1][6]

Asian brands, especially Japanese ones, use the PA system, based on a persistent pigment darkening reaction: PA+ corresponds to a UVA protection factor of about 2 to 4, PA++ to 4 to 8, PA+++ to above 8, and PA++++, added in 2013, to 16 or above.[4] Wikipedia notes that conventional sunscreen can block little UVA relative to its nominal SPF, which is why broad-spectrum labelling exists.[4]

In the United States, the FDA's broad-spectrum rule effective from 2012 requires UVA protection proportional to UVB protection. The FDA proposed adopting a version of the Boots star system in 2007 but did not, reportedly out of concern that it would confuse consumers.[1]

A 2011 study of fifteen European sunscreens with the same labelled SPF found differences in photoprotection under natural sunlight, and called for global harmonisation of photostability and UVA labelling.[2] A 2008 study assessed UVA protection in vitro of 13 popular U.S. sunscreens at a time when the U.S. had no UVA testing or labelling regulation.[3] A history review describes how sunscreen filters and regulation have evolved with understanding of UVA, UVB and visible light.[5]
No studies found that evaluate the Boots star rating itself in people. Related laboratory work on UVA protection is cited above.[2][3]

timeline.event: Franz Greiter introduces the SPF concept; the star rating is later developed by Boots from Brian Diffey's work.[4]
European Commission Recommendation 2006/647/EC sets the one-third UVA rule.[1]
In August the FDA proposes a version of the star protocol and does not adopt it.[4]
FDA broad-spectrum labelling rules take effect.[1]
PA++++ category added to the PA system in East Asia.[4]

card.summary: UK/Ireland star label showing a sunscreen's UVA-to-UVB protection ratio, from Boots.
card.note: Stars describe UVA ratio, not total protection; read SPF as well.

quick.overview:
The Boots star rating is a UK and Ireland label for the ratio of UVA to UVB protection in a sunscreen.

It runs up to five stars and was developed with Brian Diffey's work.
quick.mechanism: An in vitro test compares UVA to UVB protection, with pre-irradiation in the revised method.
quick.risks: Studies note labelling differences between regions and products with identical SPF.
